Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: What primary purpose does the preparation of a Trial Balance serve in bookkeeping?
Option A: To evaluate the operational efficiency and solvency of the business
Option B: To calculate the net profit or loss of the enterprise
Option C: To determine the exact market value of all enterprise assets
Option D: To check the arithmetical accuracy of transactions recorded and posted
Hint: Consider what mathematical or clerical check is performed after ledger balances are drawn.
Explanation: A Trial Balance is prepared specifically to check the arithmetical accuracy of transactions recorded in a Journal, posted into the ledger, and balanced. Evaluating profit is done via the Profit and Loss Account.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Why is the agreement of a Trial Balance considered only partial proof of accounting accuracy?
Option A: Because the Trial Balance does not take cash balances into consideration
Option B: Because it only records personal accounts and ignores nominal accounts
Option C: Because certain errors may still exist even if both sides of the Trial Balance tally
Option D: Because a Trial Balance is prepared before journal entries are finalized
Hint: Think about errors that do not affect the debit and credit equality.
Explanation: Even if a Trial Balance agrees, there may still be errors such as errors of complete omission, principle, or compensating errors in the accounting records. Hence, agreement is only partial proof.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: According to the chapter, which of the following is an unavoidable reality in accounting despite shifting from manual to computerized systems?
Option A: Calculation of depreciation
Option B: Valuation of closing stock
Option C: Preparation of vouchers
Option D: Occurrence of errors in accounting records
Hint: Recall what the text notes about human input and system shifts in modern business.
Explanation: The chapter highlights that even though many business units have shifted to computerized accounting, errors in accounting are unavoidable and must be located and rectified.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Which of the following is NOT listed in the chapter as a primary reason for the occurrence of errors?
Option A: Lack of accounting knowledge
Option B: Incorrect arithmetical calculations
Option C: Fluctuations in market exchange rates
Option D: Wrong data collections and wrong recording
Hint: Identify the external economic factor rather than an internal bookkeeping clerical mistake.
Explanation: The four reasons for errors listed in the chapter are: lack of accounting knowledge, wrong data collection, wrong recording, and incorrect arithmetical calculations. Market rate fluctuations are external economic changes, not bookkeeping errors.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Rectification of errors is fundamentally necessary prior to finalizing financial statements in order to:
Option A: Artificially inflate gross profit to secure bank financing
Option B: Avoid making ledger postings into the nominal accounts
Option C: Eliminate the requirement of auditing books of accounts
Option D: Find out the real profit or loss and determine the accurate financial position
Hint: Look at the core objectives mentioned under the 'Need of Rectification' section.
Explanation: Errors must be located and rectified so that corrected figures are used to prepare the Profit & Loss Account (finding true profit/loss) and Balance Sheet (showing the true financial position).

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Which of the following represents the four broad categories of errors classified in the chapter?
Option A: Clerical errors, Systemic errors, Primary errors, and Secondary errors
Option B: Single entry errors, Double entry errors, Balance Sheet errors, and Profit errors
Option C: Internal errors, External errors, Valuation errors, and Estimation errors
Option D: Errors of Omission, Errors of Commission, Errors of Principle, and Compensating Errors
Hint: Focus on the classification diagram presented on page 249 of the chapter.
Explanation: The textbook classifies errors into four main categories: Errors of Omission, Errors of Commission, Errors of Principle, and Compensating Errors.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: What is an Error of Omission?
Option A: Committing an arithmetical mistake in calculating compound interest
Option B: Recording a transaction on the correct side but in a wrong class of account
Option C: An error arising when a transaction is partially or completely omitted from being recorded
Option D: Posting an entry twice to both the debit and credit sides
Hint: Think of the root word 'omit'—forgetting to record either part or whole of a transaction.
Explanation: An error of omission arises when a transaction is partially or completely omitted to be recorded in the books of accounts.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Goods sold to Aditya on credit were completely omitted from the Sales Book. What impact will this error have on the Trial Balance?
Option A: The Trial Balance debit column will exceed the credit column by the sales amount
Option B: The Trial Balance credit column will exceed the debit column
Option C: The agreement of the Trial Balance will not be affected
Option D: The Trial Balance will fail to agree and require a Suspense Account
Hint: Consider whether any debit or credit entry was made in any ledger account.
Explanation: In an error of complete omission, neither the debit entry nor the credit entry is posted. Because both sides are equally missing, the agreement of the Trial Balance is not affected.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Goods sold to Aditya on credit were recorded in the Sales Book but not posted to Aditya's Account. This is an example of:
Option A: Partial omission
Option B: Error of principle
Option C: Error of complete omission
Option D: Compensating error
Hint: Notice that one aspect of the transaction was processed while the other was omitted.
Explanation: When a transaction is recorded in the subsidiary book (Sales Book) so Sales A/c is credited, but omitted from being posted to the customer's personal account, it is a partial omission and affects the Trial Balance.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Which of the following errors is classified as an Error of Commission?
Option A: Complete omission of credit purchases from the Purchase Book
Option B: Repairs to old building debited to Building Account
Option C: Wrong totalling or wrong balancing of ledger accounts
Option D: Wages paid for installation of machinery debited to Wages Account
Hint: Errors of commission are clerical mistakes involving recording, posting, casting, or carrying forward.
Explanation: Errors of commission arise due to wrong entries, wrong posting, wrong totalling, wrong balancing, or wrong casting. Violating capital vs revenue distinctions is an error of principle.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Goods purchased from Chaitanya for ₹850 were recorded as ₹580 in the Purchase Book. What is the effect of this error on the Trial Balance?
Option A: The Trial Balance will show an excess credit of ₹270
Option B: The Trial Balance will show an excess debit of ₹270
Option C: The Trial Balance will be out of balance by ₹850
Option D: It will not affect the agreement of the Trial Balance
Hint: Check what amount gets posted to both the Purchase Account and Chaitanya's Account.
Explanation: Because the wrong amount (₹580) was entered in the book of original entry (Purchase Book), the same amount is posted to both the debit of Purchase A/c and credit of Chaitanya's A/c, leaving the Trial Balance in agreement.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: If the Purchase Book has been undercast by ₹500, how does it immediately affect the Trial Balance?
Option A: Trial Balance will still balance without any difference
Option B: Debit side of the Trial Balance will be more by ₹500
Option C: Credit side of the Trial Balance will be less by ₹500
Option D: Debit side of the Trial Balance will be less by ₹500
Hint: The total of the Purchase Book is posted to the debit of the Purchase Account.
Explanation: Undercasting the Purchase Book means its periodic total is short by ₹500. This results in Purchase A/c being debited less by ₹500, decreasing the debit side of the Trial Balance by ₹500.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: When a Creditors Account in the ledger has been undercast by ₹700, what is the resulting effect on the Trial Balance?
Option A: Both debit and credit totals will increase by ₹700
Option B: Debit balance of Trial Balance will be less by ₹700
Option C: Credit balance of Trial Balance will be less by ₹700
Option D: Credit balance of Trial Balance will be more by ₹700
Hint: Creditors maintain a credit balance in the ledger.
Explanation: Creditors account normally has a credit balance. If it is undercast by ₹700, its credit balance is reported short by ₹700, causing the credit total of the Trial Balance to be less by ₹700.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: The total of the Purchase Book of ₹1,500 is carried forward as ₹1,250 to the next page. What type of clerical error is this?
Option A: Error of complete omission
Option B: Compensating error
Option C: Error of principle
Option D: Error of carrying forward
Hint: Look at the specific sub-type of commission error where page totals are forwarded.
Explanation: Carrying forward a total incorrectly from one page to the next (₹1,500 carried forward as ₹1,250) is specifically classified as an Error of Carrying Forward under errors of commission.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Goods sold to Rohan for ₹900 were posted to the credit of Rohan's Account instead of his debit side. What type of posting error has occurred?
Option A: Posting to the wrong side but correct account
Option B: Posting to the correct side but wrong account
Option C: Complete omission of posting
Option D: Posting twice in an account
Hint: Identify whether the account name was correct and what side received the entry.
Explanation: Rohan's account was correctly identified, but the amount was posted to the credit side instead of the debit side, which is 'Posting to the wrong side but correct account'.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: What is an Error of Principle?
Option A: Carrying forward an incorrect page balance in a subsidiary book
Option B: Recording transactions without following accounting principles and rules, such as confusing capital and revenue items
Option C: An arithmetical error where debit mistakes equal credit mistakes
Option D: A clerical omission of posting a journal entry to the ledger
Hint: Think about fundamental accounting concepts like capital vs revenue expenditure.
Explanation: Transactions recorded without following accounting principles and rules (especially incorrect classification between capital and revenue) are known as Errors of Principle.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Wages paid for the installation of new machinery were debited to Wages Account instead of Machinery Account. Does this error affect the Trial Balance?
Option A: Yes, because Wages Account has a higher debit balance
Option B: No, because both cash and machinery are asset accounts
Option C: Yes, because installation wages cannot be debited anywhere
Option D: No, because a debit was still made for the correct amount, though in the wrong account
Hint: Check whether equal debits and credits were placed in the ledger books.
Explanation: An error of principle does not affect the Trial Balance because the debit amount was placed on the correct side (debit), even though it was charged to an incorrect account (Wages instead of Machinery).

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: An amount of ₹500 paid for repairs to old machinery was debited to Machinery Account instead of Repairs Account. This is an example of:
Option A: Treating Capital expenditure as Revenue expenditure
Option B: Compensating error
Option C: Treating Revenue expenditure as Capital expenditure
Option D: Error of partial omission
Hint: Repairs are routine operational expenses, whereas Machinery is a fixed asset.
Explanation: Routine repair of old machinery is a revenue expenditure. Debiting it to Machinery Account treats a revenue item as a capital item, violating accounting principles.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Which of the following defines Compensating Errors?
Option A: Errors that are automatically rectified at the end of the year by closing entries
Option B: Errors resulting strictly from the ignorance of capital and revenue distinctions
Option C: Errors that occur when a single transaction is entered twice in the journal
Option D: Errors where two or more mistakes are committed such that their net effect on debit and credit is nil
Hint: Notice how one error offsets or counterbalances the effect of another.
Explanation: Compensating errors occur when two or more errors are committed in such a way that the net effect of these errors on the debit and credit of accounts is nil or nullified.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: A sum of ₹3,000 paid to Ashok was posted as ₹300 to his debit, and ₹300 paid to Kumar was posted as ₹3,000 to his debit. What type of error is this?
Option A: Compensating error
Option B: Error of principle
Option C: Error of complete omission
Option D: Partial omission
Hint: Ashok's debit was short by ₹2,700, while Kumar's debit was excess by ₹2,700.
Explanation: The under-debit of ₹2,700 in Ashok's account is counterbalanced by an over-debit of ₹2,700 in Kumar's account, making the net effect on the debit total zero. This is a compensating error.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: What is the key distinguishing characteristic of a One-Sided Error?
Option A: It affects only one account and affects the agreement of the Trial Balance
Option B: It arises solely from treating capital items as revenue items
Option C: It can never be rectified once books are closed
Option D: It affects two or more accounts and does not affect the Trial Balance
Hint: Consider how many accounts are touched and whether debits still equal credits.
Explanation: One-sided errors affect only one account and consequently disturb the agreement of the Trial Balance.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: How is a one-sided error rectified if it is located BEFORE the preparation of the Trial Balance?
Option A: By giving an explanatory note for debiting or crediting the affected account in the ledger
Option B: By directly adjusting the proprietor's Capital Account
Option C: By passing a compound journal entry in the Cash Book
Option D: By opening a temporary Suspense Account
Hint: At this stage, no Trial Balance or Suspense Account has been created yet.
Explanation: If a one-sided error is located before preparing the Trial Balance, no journal entry through Suspense Account is passed; it is rectified simply by writing an explanatory note to debit or credit the affected account.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: When one-sided errors are located AFTER the preparation of the Trial Balance, they are rectified with the help of:
Option A: Trading Account
Option B: Reserve Fund Account
Option C: Profit & Loss Appropriation Account
Option D: Suspense Account
Hint: Recall the temporary holding account created when a Trial Balance does not balance.
Explanation: When one-sided errors are detected after the Trial Balance has been prepared, the discrepancy in the Trial Balance is held in a Suspense Account, which is used to pass rectifying journal entries.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: In which book of original entry are rectification journal entries recorded?
Option A: Purchase Book
Option B: Sales Book
Option C: Journal Proper
Option D: Cash Book
Hint: This subsidiary book is reserved for entries that cannot be accommodated in specialized day books.
Explanation: As noted explicitly in the chapter: 'Rectified entries are recorded in Journal Proper.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Which formula is provided in the chapter's working notes to determine a Rectifying Entry for two-sided errors?
Option A: Rectifying Entry = Correct Entry - Reverse Entry
Option B: Rectifying Entry = Reverse Entry + Correct Entry
Option C: Rectifying Entry = Wrong Entry + Correct Entry
Option D: Rectifying Entry = Suspense Entry + Cash Entry
Hint: To cancel a wrong entry, you reverse it, and then you combine it with the correct entry.
Explanation: The textbook explicitly states the working note formula: 'Rectifying Entry = Reverse Entry + Correct Entry'.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: According to Section 8.3 of the chapter, what are the three distinct stages of detecting errors?
Option A: During recording, During posting, and During balancing
Option B: Internal audit stage, External audit stage, and Tax assessment stage
Option C: Before Trial Balance; After Trial Balance but before Final Accounts; and After Final Accounts
Option D: Before Journalizing; Before Ledger Posting; and Before Vouching
Hint: Look at the timeline relative to Trial Balance preparation and final accounts closure.
Explanation: Section 8.3 defines the three stages as: Stage 1 - Before preparation of Trial Balance; Stage 2 - After preparation of the Trial Balance but before preparing Final Accounts; Stage 3 - After preparing Final Accounts.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: According to the 'Effects of Errors' diagram in the chapter, accounting errors directly impact which three core components?
Option A: Sales Book, Purchase Book, and Journal Proper
Option B: Inventory Ledger, Asset Register, and Payroll
Option C: Cash Flow, Bank Statement, and Pass Book
Option D: Trial Balance, Profit & Loss Account, and Balance Sheet
Hint: Look at the triangular diagram illustrated on page 256.
Explanation: The Effects of Errors triangle shows Trial Balance at the apex, with Profit & Loss Account and Balance Sheet at the base corners.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Salaries of ₹2,500 paid to Shrikant were wrongly debited to his personal account in the ledger. What is the correct rectifying entry?
Option A: Debit Shrikant's A/c ₹2,500; Credit Cash A/c ₹2,500
Option B: Debit Shrikant's A/c ₹2,500; Credit Salary A/c ₹2,500
Option C: Debit Salary A/c ₹2,500; Credit Shrikant's A/c ₹2,500
Option D: Debit Salary A/c ₹2,500; Credit Suspense A/c ₹2,500
Hint: Salary is an expense that should be debited; Shrikant's personal account was wrongly debited and must now be credited to cancel it.
Explanation: The correct debit should have been to Salary Account. Since Shrikant's personal account was wrongly debited, crediting Shrikant's A/c cancels the error and debiting Salary A/c establishes the expense.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Sale of old furniture for ₹2,000 was wrongly recorded as a sale of goods (credited to Sales Account). What is the rectifying journal entry?
Option A: Debit Sales A/c ₹2,000; Credit Suspense A/c ₹2,000
Option B: Debit Furniture A/c ₹2,000; Credit Sales A/c ₹2,000
Option C: Debit Sales A/c ₹2,000; Credit Furniture A/c ₹2,000
Option D: Debit Cash A/c ₹2,000; Credit Furniture A/c ₹2,000
Hint: Sales Account was wrongly credited and must be debited; Furniture Account should have been credited.
Explanation: Selling an asset should reduce the asset balance (Credit Furniture A/c). Because Sales A/c was wrongly credited, it must be debited by ₹2,000 to reverse it, and Furniture A/c credited by ₹2,000.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: An amount of ₹7,000 withdrawn by the proprietor for personal use was debited to Trade Expenses Account. How is this error rectified?
Option A: Debit Drawings A/c ₹7,000; Credit Trade Expenses A/c ₹7,000
Option B: Debit Trade Expenses A/c ₹7,000; Credit Drawings A/c ₹7,000
Option C: Debit Drawings A/c ₹7,000; Credit Cash A/c ₹7,000
Option D: Debit Capital A/c ₹7,000; Credit Suspense A/c ₹7,000
Hint: Personal withdrawals belong to Drawings, not operating trade expenses.
Explanation: Drawings Account should have been debited. To remove the incorrect debit from Trade Expenses Account, credit Trade Expenses A/c ₹7,000 and debit Drawings A/c ₹7,000.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Cash received from Mr. Sawant ₹500 was wrongly credited to Mr. Shinde's Account. What is the journal entry to rectify this mistake?
Option A: Debit Cash A/c ₹500; Credit Sawant A/c ₹500
Option B: Debit Shinde A/c ₹500; Credit Sawant A/c ₹500
Option C: Debit Shinde A/c ₹500; Credit Cash A/c ₹500
Option D: Debit Sawant A/c ₹500; Credit Shinde A/c ₹500
Hint: Debit the person who was mistakenly credited, and credit the actual payer.
Explanation: Mr. Shinde was mistakenly credited; therefore, Shinde's A/c must be debited with ₹500 to cancel the credit. Mr. Sawant gave the cash, so Sawant's A/c must be credited with ₹500.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: An amount of ₹1,500 received as interest was wrongly credited to Commission Account. What is the proper rectifying entry?
Option A: Debit Commission A/c ₹1,500; Credit Interest A/c ₹1,500
Option B: Debit Commission A/c ₹1,500; Credit Suspense A/c ₹1,500
Option C: Debit Cash A/c ₹1,500; Credit Interest A/c ₹1,500
Option D: Debit Interest A/c ₹1,500; Credit Commission A/c ₹1,500
Hint: Cancel the wrong income credit by debiting it, then credit the true income account.
Explanation: Commission Account was credited by mistake, so it must be debited by ₹1,500. The correct revenue account to credit is Interest Account for ₹1,500.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: A payment of ₹5,000 for the purchase of a computer was charged to Office Expenses Account. What entry rectifies this error of principle?
Option A: Debit Computer A/c ₹5,000; Credit Office Expenses A/c ₹5,000
Option B: Debit Office Expenses A/c ₹5,000; Credit Computer A/c ₹5,000
Option C: Debit Computer A/c ₹5,000; Credit Cash A/c ₹5,000
Option D: Debit Purchases A/c ₹5,000; Credit Computer A/c ₹5,000
Hint: A computer is a capital asset, not an operational office expense.
Explanation: The computer is an asset and must be debited. The incorrect debit to Office Expenses A/c is eliminated by crediting Office Expenses A/c by ₹5,000.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Carriage paid of ₹500 on the purchase of a new machine was debited to Carriage Account. What rectifying entry is needed?
Option A: Debit Carriage A/c ₹500; Credit Cash A/c ₹500
Option B: Debit Carriage A/c ₹500; Credit Machinery A/c ₹500
Option C: Debit Machinery A/c ₹500; Credit Carriage A/c ₹500
Option D: Debit Machinery A/c ₹500; Credit Cash A/c ₹500
Hint: Carriage incurred to bring a new machine to the premises is capitalized into the asset cost.
Explanation: Expenses incurred on acquiring and installing a capital asset must be capitalized to the asset account. Hence, Machinery A/c is debited and Carriage A/c is credited with ₹500.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Before the preparation of the Trial Balance, it was found that the Return Inward Book was overcast by ₹200. How should this error be rectified?
Option A: By passing a journal entry: Suspense A/c Dr. ₹200 to Return Inward A/c ₹200
Option B: By passing a journal entry: Return Inward A/c Dr. ₹200 to Debtors A/c ₹200
Option C: No journal entry is required; Return Inwards A/c is simply credited with ₹200 in the ledger
Option D: No journal entry is required; Return Inwards A/c is debited with ₹200 in the ledger
Hint: Before the Trial Balance, single-sided errors are corrected by an explanatory ledger note.
Explanation: Before the Trial Balance is prepared, single-account errors require no journal entry. Return Inward normally has a debit balance; being overcast (excess debit), it is corrected by crediting Returns Inwards A/c with ₹200.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Goods sold to Mr. Abhiraj for ₹350 were wrongly entered in the Purchases Day Book as ₹530. What is the correct rectifying journal entry?
Option A: Debit Purchases A/c ₹530; Credit Sales A/c ₹350; Credit Abhiraj A/c ₹180
Option B: Debit Abhiraj A/c ₹180; Credit Suspense A/c ₹180
Option C: Debit Sales A/c ₹350; Debit Purchases A/c ₹530; Credit Abhiraj A/c ₹880
Option D: Debit Abhiraj A/c ₹880; Credit Purchases A/c ₹530; Credit Sales A/c ₹350
Hint: Abhiraj should be debited with ₹350, Purchases wrongly debited with ₹530 must be credited, and Sales must be credited with ₹350.
Explanation: To rectify: Reverse the wrong purchase debit by crediting Purchases A/c ₹530. Record the true credit sale by crediting Sales A/c ₹350. Debit Abhiraj with the total (₹530 wrongly credited + ₹350 correct debit = ₹880).

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Before the Trial Balance is prepared, commission received of ₹200 was posted to the debit of Commission Account instead of its credit. How should it be rectified?
Option A: Credit Commission Account with ₹200 in the ledger
Option B: Credit Commission Account with ₹400 in the ledger
Option C: Debit Commission Account with ₹400 in the ledger
Option D: Pass a journal entry: Commission A/c Dr. ₹400 to Suspense A/c ₹400
Hint: A wrong debit of ₹200 requires ₹200 to neutralize plus ₹200 to record the actual credit.
Explanation: Because this one-sided error is detected before the Trial Balance, no journal entry is passed. To cancel the wrong debit of ₹200 and provide the required credit of ₹200, Commission A/c is credited with ₹400.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: A cheque for ₹320 issued to Mr. Ram was wrongly entered in the cash column of the Cash Book instead of the bank column. What is the rectifying entry?
Option A: Debit Cash A/c ₹320; Credit Bank A/c ₹320
Option B: Debit Ram A/c ₹320; Credit Bank A/c ₹320
Option C: Debit Bank A/c ₹320; Credit Cash A/c ₹320
Option D: Debit Cash A/c ₹320; Credit Ram A/c ₹320
Hint: Cash was credited when bank should have been credited. To cancel cash credit, debit cash.
Explanation: Entering a cheque payment in the cash column credited Cash Account instead of Bank Account. To correct this, Cash A/c is debited with ₹320 (restoring cash) and Bank A/c is credited with ₹320.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: A factory electricity bill of ₹7,000 paid in cash was recorded twice in the books. What is the rectifying entry?
Option A: Debit Factory Electricity A/c ₹7,000; Credit Cash A/c ₹7,000
Option B: Debit Cash A/c ₹7,000; Credit Factory Electricity A/c ₹7,000
Option C: Debit Factory Electricity A/c ₹14,000; Credit Cash A/c ₹14,000
Option D: Debit Suspense A/c ₹7,000; Credit Factory Electricity A/c ₹7,000
Hint: To reverse an entire duplicate payment entry, flip the original entry once.
Explanation: Since the entry was made twice (two debits to Electricity and two credits to Cash), reversing one instance by debiting Cash A/c ₹7,000 and crediting Factory Electricity A/c ₹7,000 rectifies the duplicate recording.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Before the Trial Balance is prepared, paid rent of ₹825 was posted to the Rent Account as ₹325. How is this error rectified?
Option A: Pass an entry: Suspense A/c Dr. ₹500 to Rent A/c ₹500
Option B: Rent Account should be credited with ₹500 by an explanatory note
Option C: Pass an entry: Rent A/c Dr. ₹500 to Suspense A/c ₹500
Option D: Rent Account should be debited with ₹500 by an explanatory note
Hint: Rent was under-debited by ₹825 - ₹325 = ₹500.
Explanation: Because this one-sided error is discovered before preparing the Trial Balance, no journal entry is required; Rent Account is simply debited with the deficit amount of ₹500.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Wages of ₹9,900 paid for the extension of an office building were charged to Wages Account. What is the rectifying entry?
Option A: Debit Repairs A/c ₹9,900; Credit Wages A/c ₹9,900
Option B: Debit Wages A/c ₹9,900; Credit Building A/c ₹9,900
Option C: Debit Building A/c ₹9,900; Credit Wages A/c ₹9,900
Option D: Debit Building A/c ₹9,900; Credit Cash A/c ₹9,900
Hint: Wages paid for extending a permanent asset must be added to the asset's value.
Explanation: Building extension is capital expenditure. The Wages Account was wrongly debited, so Building A/c must be debited by ₹9,900 and Wages A/c credited by ₹9,900 to rectify the error of principle.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Life insurance premium of the proprietor amounting to ₹1,500 was wrongly debited to Insurance Account. What is the proper rectifying entry?
Option A: Debit Drawings A/c ₹1,500; Credit Cash A/c ₹1,500
Option B: Debit Insurance A/c ₹1,500; Credit Drawings A/c ₹1,500
Option C: Debit Drawings A/c ₹1,500; Credit Insurance A/c ₹1,500
Option D: Debit Profit and Loss A/c ₹1,500; Credit Insurance A/c ₹1,500
Hint: A life insurance policy for the owner is a personal expense, not a business risk policy.
Explanation: The life insurance premium of the proprietor is a personal expense treated as Drawings. Debiting Insurance A/c treated it as a business expense; hence, debit Drawings A/c ₹1,500 and credit Insurance A/c ₹1,500.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Goods of ₹2,000 returned by Sumit & Co. were included in stock, but no entry was passed in the books. What is the rectifying entry?
Option A: Debit Stock A/c ₹2,000; Credit Purchases A/c ₹2,000
Option B: Debit Sumit & Co. ₹2,000; Credit Sales Return A/c ₹2,000
Option C: Debit Purchases Return A/c ₹2,000; Credit Sumit & Co. ₹2,000
Option D: Debit Sales Return A/c ₹2,000; Credit Sumit & Co. ₹2,000
Hint: Goods returned by a customer represent Sales Return (Return Inward).
Explanation: Returns by customers are Sales Returns. Complete omission is rectified by recording the original entry: Debit Sales Return A/c ₹2,000 and Credit Sumit & Co. ₹2,000.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Goods purchased for ₹1,200 were erroneously entered in the Purchases Book as ₹12,000. What is the rectifying journal entry?
Option A: Debit Suspense A/c ₹10,800; Credit Purchases A/c ₹10,800
Option B: Debit Creditors A/c ₹10,800; Credit Purchases A/c ₹10,800
Option C: Debit Creditors A/c ₹12,000; Credit Purchases A/c ₹1,200; Credit Suspense A/c ₹10,800
Option D: Debit Purchases A/c ₹10,800; Credit Creditors A/c ₹10,800
Hint: Both Purchases and Creditors were overstated by ₹12,000 - ₹1,200 = ₹10,800.
Explanation: Entering ₹12,000 instead of ₹1,200 caused Purchases to be debited excess by ₹10,800 and Creditors to be credited excess by ₹10,800. The reversal entry is: Debit Creditors A/c ₹10,800 and Credit Purchases A/c ₹10,800.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Goods purchased from Sujit for ₹3,000 were recorded in the Sales Book. What is the rectifying journal entry?
Option A: Debit Purchases A/c ₹3,000; Credit Sales A/c ₹3,000
Option B: Debit Purchases A/c ₹3,000, Debit Sales A/c ₹3,000; Credit Sujit's A/c ₹6,000
Option C: Debit Purchases A/c ₹3,000; Credit Sujit's A/c ₹3,000
Option D: Debit Sujit's A/c ₹6,000; Credit Purchases A/c ₹3,000, Credit Sales A/c ₹3,000
Hint: You must record the purchase debit, cancel the sales credit, and credit Sujit with the combined amount.
Explanation: Purchases A/c must be debited by ₹3,000. Sales A/c was wrongly credited by ₹3,000, so it must be debited by ₹3,000. Sujit's A/c was wrongly debited by ₹3,000 and should have been credited by ₹3,000, so Sujit is credited with ₹6,000.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Goods for ₹5,200 sold to Sachin were mistakenly passed through the Purchase Book. What is the rectifying entry?
Option A: Debit Purchases A/c ₹5,200, Debit Sales A/c ₹5,200; Credit Sachin's A/c ₹10,400
Option B: Debit Sachin's A/c ₹10,400; Credit Sales A/c ₹5,200, Credit Purchases A/c ₹5,200
Option C: Debit Sachin's A/c ₹5,200; Credit Purchases A/c ₹5,200
Option D: Debit Sachin's A/c ₹5,200; Credit Sales A/c ₹5,200
Hint: Sachin's credit of ₹5,200 from purchase book must be undone and he must be debited for the sale.
Explanation: The rectifying entry debits Sachin's A/c by ₹10,400 (₹5,200 to cancel the wrong credit + ₹5,200 for the actual sale debit) and credits Sales A/c ₹5,200 and Purchases A/c ₹5,200 (to cancel wrong purchase debit).

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: A customer returned goods worth ₹800, but the return was recorded in the Purchase Return Book. What is the rectifying journal entry?
Option A: Debit Purchases Return A/c ₹800; Credit Customer's A/c ₹800
Option B: Debit Customer's A/c ₹1,600; Credit Sales Return A/c ₹800, Credit Purchases Return A/c ₹800
Option C: Debit Sales Return A/c ₹800; Credit Purchases Return A/c ₹800
Option D: Debit Sales Return A/c ₹800, Debit Purchases Return A/c ₹800; Credit Customer's A/c ₹1,600
Hint: Sales Return must be debited, Purchase Return credit must be cancelled by debiting it, and Customer must be credited.
Explanation: Sales Return A/c is debited ₹800 to record the inward return; Purchases Return A/c is debited ₹800 to cancel the incorrect credit; Customer's A/c is credited ₹1,600 (canceling the wrong debit and posting the true credit).

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: A credit sale of ₹240 to Ajit was entered in the Sales Book as ₹420. What is the rectifying entry?
Option A: Debit Ajit's A/c ₹180; Credit Sales A/c ₹180
Option B: Debit Sales A/c ₹420; Credit Ajit's A/c ₹420
Option C: Debit Sales A/c ₹180; Credit Ajit's A/c ₹180
Option D: Debit Suspense A/c ₹180; Credit Sales A/c ₹180
Hint: Sales and customer were both overstated by ₹420 - ₹240 = ₹180.
Explanation: Both Sales A/c and Ajit's A/c were overstated by ₹180 (₹420 - ₹240). Reversing the excess requires debiting Sales A/c with ₹180 and crediting Ajit's A/c with ₹180.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: When the credit total of a Trial Balance is higher than the debit total, to which side of the Suspense Account is the difference transferred?
Option A: Directly to the Profit and Loss Account
Option B: Debit side
Option C: Credit side
Option D: Neither side; it is transferred to Capital Account
Hint: The difference is placed on the lighter side to make the columns tally temporarily.
Explanation: When the credit column total is higher than the debit column total, the shortage is on the debit side; hence, the difference is placed on the debit side of the Suspense Account.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: What happens to the Suspense Account once all one-sided errors have been located and rectified?
Option A: It permanently maintains a debit balance transferred to the Balance Sheet
Option B: Its balance is transferred to General Reserve
Option C: It is converted into a Nominal Account
Option D: It automatically closes with a nil balance
Hint: Suspense Account is purely a temporary holding account for discrepancies.
Explanation: As stated in Section 8.4: 'When all one sided errors are located and rectified Suspense Account automatically closes.'

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: An amount of ₹840 received from M/s Singh & Co. was posted to their debit as ₹50. What is the rectifying entry through Suspense Account?
Option A: Debit Suspense A/c ₹790; Credit M/s Singh & Co. ₹790
Option B: Debit M/s Singh & Co. ₹890; Credit Suspense A/c ₹890
Option C: Debit Cash A/c ₹840; Credit M/s Singh & Co. ₹840
Option D: Debit Suspense A/c ₹890; Credit M/s Singh & Co. ₹890
Hint: Singh & Co. needs a credit of ₹50 to clear the wrong debit, plus ₹840 for the true credit.
Explanation: Singh & Co. should have been credited with ₹840, but was debited with ₹50. To correct their account, they must be credited with ₹50 + ₹840 = ₹890, and Suspense Account is debited with ₹890.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: ₹530 spent for repairs to machinery was posted to the debit of Machinery Account as ₹150. What is the rectifying entry through Suspense Account?
Option A: Repairs to Machinery A/c Dr. ₹380; To Suspense A/c ₹380
Option B: Suspense A/c Dr. ₹380; To Machinery A/c ₹380
Option C: Machinery A/c Dr. ₹380; To Repairs to Machinery A/c ₹380
Option D: Repairs to Machinery A/c Dr. ₹530; To Machinery A/c ₹150, To Suspense A/c ₹380
Hint: Debit Repairs with full ₹530, credit Machinery with ₹150 to remove wrong debit, and balance with Suspense.
Explanation: Repairs Account must be debited with the actual amount ₹530. The incorrect debit of ₹150 in Machinery Account is cancelled by crediting Machinery A/c ₹150. The remaining difference of ₹380 is credited to Suspense A/c.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: A discount of ₹25 allowed by Shah & Co. to us (discount received) was posted to their credit. What is the rectifying entry using Suspense Account?
Option A: Debit Shah & Co. ₹50; Credit Suspense A/c ₹50
Option B: Debit Discount Allowed A/c ₹25; Credit Shah & Co. ₹25
Option C: Debit Shah & Co. ₹25; Credit Discount Received A/c ₹25
Option D: Debit Suspense A/c ₹50; Credit Shah & Co. ₹50
Hint: Shah & Co. should have been debited by ₹25, but was credited by ₹25.
Explanation: Shah & Co. should be debited by ₹25 to cancel the incorrect credit and debited another ₹25 to record the proper discount debit (total debit ₹50). The corresponding credit goes to Suspense Account for ₹50.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: An amount of ₹730 paid to Chetan & Co. was wrongly credited to Lalit & Co. as ₹250. What entry rectifies this mistake via Suspense Account?
Option A: Chetan & Co. Dr. ₹730, Lalit & Co. Dr. ₹250; To Suspense A/c ₹980
Option B: Chetan & Co. Dr. ₹730; To Lalit & Co. ₹250, To Suspense A/c ₹480
Option C: Lalit & Co. Dr. ₹250; To Chetan & Co. ₹250
Option D: Suspense A/c Dr. ₹980; To Chetan & Co. ₹730, To Lalit & Co. ₹250
Hint: Debit Chetan & Co. ₹730, cancel Lalit & Co.'s credit by debiting ₹250, and credit the total to Suspense.
Explanation: Chetan & Co. was not debited, so debit Chetan & Co. ₹730. Lalit & Co. was mistakenly credited with ₹250, so debit Lalit & Co. ₹250. Credit Suspense Account with the total ₹980.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: The total of Purchase Returns Book of ₹3,150 was carried forward as ₹1,530. What is the rectifying entry through Suspense Account?
Option A: Debit Purchase Return A/c ₹3,150; Credit Suspense A/c ₹3,150
Option B: Debit Suspense A/c ₹1,620; Credit Purchase Return A/c ₹1,620
Option C: Debit Suspense A/c ₹1,530; Credit Purchase Return A/c ₹1,530
Option D: Debit Purchase Return A/c ₹1,620; Credit Suspense A/c ₹1,620
Hint: Purchase Return Book has a credit balance; it was under-credited by ₹3,150 - ₹1,530 = ₹1,620.
Explanation: Purchase Return Book has a normal credit total. Carrying forward ₹1,530 instead of ₹3,150 undercast the credit by ₹1,620. To rectify, Purchase Return A/c is credited ₹1,620 and Suspense A/c is debited ₹1,620.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Cash paid to Shweta ₹7,500 was debited to Ankita's Account as ₹7,000. What is the rectifying journal entry?
Option A: Debit Shweta's A/c ₹7,500; Credit Ankita's A/c ₹7,000, Credit Suspense A/c ₹500
Option B: Debit Shweta's A/c ₹500; Credit Suspense A/c ₹500
Option C: Debit Shweta's A/c ₹7,500; Credit Ankita's A/c ₹7,500
Option D: Debit Ankita's A/c ₹7,000, Debit Suspense A/c ₹500; Credit Shweta's A/c ₹7,500
Hint: Shweta needs a debit of ₹7,500; Ankita's debit of ₹7,000 must be cancelled by credit; difference goes to Suspense.
Explanation: Shweta's Account must be debited with the correct payment ₹7,500. Ankita's account was wrongly debited with ₹7,000, so credit Ankita's A/c ₹7,000. The ₹500 shortage on the credit side is posted to Suspense A/c.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Amount paid on the registration of a newly acquired motor car of ₹800 was recorded as legal charges. What is the rectifying journal entry?
Option A: Debit Motor Car A/c ₹800; Credit Legal Charges A/c ₹800
Option B: Debit Legal Charges A/c ₹800; Credit Motor Car A/c ₹800
Option C: Debit Motor Car A/c ₹800; Credit Cash A/c ₹800
Option D: Debit Motor Car A/c ₹800; Credit Suspense A/c ₹800
Hint: Registration charges on a vehicle acquisition must be capitalized to the vehicle account.
Explanation: Registration expenses of a motor car are capital expenditures to be added to Motor Car Account. To remove the incorrect charge to Legal Charges Account, credit Legal Charges A/c ₹800 and debit Motor Car A/c ₹800.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Repairs of ₹1,000 paid for overhauling a second-hand machine purchased were debited to Repairs Account. What is the correct rectifying entry?
Option A: Debit Repairs A/c ₹1,000; Credit Machinery A/c ₹1,000
Option B: Debit Machinery A/c ₹1,000; Credit Cash A/c ₹1,000
Option C: Debit Suspense A/c ₹1,000; Credit Repairs A/c ₹1,000
Option D: Debit Machinery A/c ₹1,000; Credit Repairs A/c ₹1,000
Hint: Overhauling a second-hand asset to put it into working condition is a capital expense.
Explanation: Cost of overhauling second-hand machinery before putting it into use is capitalized into Machinery Account. Debiting Repairs was an error of principle, rectified by debiting Machinery A/c ₹1,000 and crediting Repairs A/c ₹1,000.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Materials worth ₹90,000 and wages of ₹10,000 used for the construction of a building were not recorded in the books. What is the rectifying entry?
Option A: Debit Building A/c ₹1,00,000; Credit Purchases A/c ₹90,000, Credit Wages A/c ₹10,000
Option B: Debit Building A/c ₹1,00,000; Credit Suspense A/c ₹1,00,000
Option C: Debit Purchases A/c ₹90,000, Debit Wages A/c ₹10,000; Credit Cash A/c ₹1,00,000
Option D: Debit Building A/c ₹1,00,000; Credit Cash A/c ₹1,00,000
Hint: Combine both material and wages into the capital asset being constructed.
Explanation: Both material (₹90,000) and wages (₹10,000) incurred on constructing a building form part of the building's capital cost. The complete omission entry is: Debit Building A/c ₹1,00,000; Credit Cash A/c ₹1,00,000.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Furniture purchased for ₹6,000 was posted to Purchases Account as ₹400. What is the rectifying entry through Suspense Account?
Option A: Debit Furniture A/c ₹5,600; Credit Suspense A/c ₹5,600
Option B: Debit Furniture A/c ₹6,000; Credit Purchases A/c ₹400, Credit Suspense A/c ₹5,600
Option C: Debit Suspense A/c ₹5,600; Credit Purchases A/c ₹5,600
Option D: Debit Furniture A/c ₹6,000; Credit Purchases A/c ₹6,000
Hint: Furniture must be debited with full ₹6,000, Purchases credit must cancel ₹400, and Suspense balances the entry.
Explanation: Furniture A/c is debited ₹6,000 (correct asset debit); Purchases A/c is credited ₹400 (reversing wrong debit); and Suspense A/c is credited with the difference of ₹5,600.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: What is the term used for taking the total more than actual while closing books of accounts?
Option A: Undercasting
Option B: Cross-casting
Option C: Balancing
Option D: Overcasting
Hint: Look at the terminology tested in Exercise Q.2(2).
Explanation: Overcasting means taking the total more than the actual sum when totalling subsidiary books or ledger accounts.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding Suspense Account?
Option A: All accounting errors can only be rectified through a Suspense Account
Option B: A Suspense Account is a permanent nominal account that appears in the Trading Account
Option C: There is no need to open a Suspense Account if the Trial Balance agrees
Option D: A Suspense Account is always opened before the Trial Balance is prepared
Hint: Suspense Account is only opened when there is a discrepancy between Trial Balance totals.
Explanation: If the Trial Balance agrees, there is no difference in totals, so no Suspense Account is opened. Furthermore, two-sided errors are rectified through Journal Proper without touching Suspense Account.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Unintentional omission or commission of amounts and accounts while recording transactions is termed as an:
Option A: Fraud
Option B: Appropriation
Option C: Error
Option D: Adjustment
Hint: Review Exercise Q.5(1) regarding unintentional bookkeeping inaccuracies.
Explanation: The unintentional omission or commission of amounts and accounts while recording transactions is defined as an error (as opposed to fraud, which is intentional).

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Purchases of goods from Siddhant Traders for ₹12,000 paid in cash was wrongly debited to Siddhant Traders Account. What is the rectifying entry?
Option A: Debit Purchases A/c ₹12,000; Credit Siddhant Traders A/c ₹12,000
Option B: Debit Purchases A/c ₹12,000; Credit Cash A/c ₹12,000
Option C: Debit Purchases A/c ₹12,000; Credit Suspense A/c ₹12,000
Option D: Debit Siddhant Traders A/c ₹12,000; Credit Purchases A/c ₹12,000
Hint: In cash purchases, the supplier's personal account is not debited; Purchases Account is debited.
Explanation: For cash purchases, Purchases A/c should be debited, not the supplier's personal account. To correct this, debit Purchases A/c ₹12,000 and credit Siddhant Traders A/c ₹12,000.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Received interest of ₹700 from Bank was wrongly credited to Bank Account instead of Interest Account. What is the rectifying journal entry?
Option A: Debit Bank A/c ₹700; Credit Interest A/c ₹700
Option B: Debit Bank A/c ₹1,400; Credit Interest A/c ₹1,400
Option C: Debit Bank A/c ₹1,400; Credit Interest A/c ₹700, Credit Suspense A/c ₹700
Option D: Debit Interest A/c ₹700; Credit Bank A/c ₹700
Hint: Bank was credited by ₹700 when it should have been debited by ₹700.
Explanation: Bank should have been debited with ₹700 (incoming interest) and Interest credited with ₹700. Since Bank was mistakenly credited with ₹700, Bank A/c must be debited with ₹1,400 to cancel the credit and record the debit, while crediting the respective revenue/rectification accounts.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: A printer purchased for ₹10,000 was wrongly passed through the Purchase Book. What is the journal entry to rectify this error?
Option A: Debit Printer A/c ₹10,000; Credit Office Expenses A/c ₹10,000
Option B: Debit Purchase A/c ₹10,000; Credit Printer A/c ₹10,000
Option C: Debit Printer A/c ₹10,000; Credit Purchase A/c ₹10,000
Option D: Debit Printer A/c ₹10,000; Credit Cash A/c ₹10,000
Hint: Printer is an office equipment/asset; Purchase Book is only for trading merchandise.
Explanation: Passing an asset purchase through the Purchase Book wrongly debited Purchases Account. Rectification requires debiting Printer A/c ₹10,000 and crediting Purchases A/c ₹10,000.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: A credit purchase of goods from Sheetal amounting to ₹2,000 was wrongly passed through the Sales Book. What is the rectifying entry?
Option A: Debit Purchases A/c ₹2,000; Credit Sheetal A/c ₹2,000
Option B: Debit Sheetal's A/c ₹4,000; Credit Purchases A/c ₹2,000, Credit Sales A/c ₹2,000
Option C: Debit Purchases A/c ₹2,000, Debit Sales A/c ₹2,000; Credit Sheetal's A/c ₹4,000
Option D: Debit Sales A/c ₹2,000; Credit Purchases A/c ₹2,000
Hint: Purchases must be debited, Sales credit cancelled by debit, and Sheetal credited for both.
Explanation: To rectify: Debit Purchases A/c ₹2,000 (recording purchase), Debit Sales A/c ₹2,000 (canceling wrong credit sale), and Credit Sheetal's A/c ₹4,000 (reversing wrong debit of ₹2,000 and crediting actual purchase of ₹2,000).

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: A return of goods worth ₹500 to Umesh was wrongly passed through the Sales Return Book. What is the rectifying journal entry?
Option A: Debit Purchase Return A/c ₹500; Credit Sales Return A/c ₹500
Option B: Debit Sales Return A/c ₹500, Debit Purchase Return A/c ₹500; Credit Umesh's A/c ₹1,000
Option C: Debit Umesh's A/c ₹500; Credit Purchase Return A/c ₹500
Option D: Debit Umesh's A/c ₹1,000; Credit Purchase Return A/c ₹500, Credit Sales Return A/c ₹500
Hint: Umesh was credited via Sales Return; he should have been debited. Also credit Purchase Return and cancel Sales Return.
Explanation: Return to Umesh is Purchase Return (credit). Entering it in Sales Return debited Sales Return and credited Umesh. To rectify: Debit Umesh ₹1,000 (₹500 to cancel credit + ₹500 correct debit), Credit Purchase Return A/c ₹500, and Credit Sales Return A/c ₹500.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: A return of goods worth ₹900 by Ganesh was entered in the Purchase Return Book. What is the rectifying entry?
Option A: Debit Sales Return A/c ₹900, Debit Purchase Return A/c ₹900; Credit Ganesh's A/c ₹1,800
Option B: Debit Purchase Return A/c ₹900; Credit Sales Return A/c ₹900
Option C: Debit Ganesh's A/c ₹1,800; Credit Sales Return A/c ₹900, Credit Purchase Return A/c ₹900
Option D: Debit Sales Return A/c ₹900; Credit Ganesh's A/c ₹900
Hint: Goods returned by a customer are Sales Returns; cancel the Purchase Return credit and credit the customer.
Explanation: Debit Sales Return A/c ₹900 to record inward return, Debit Purchase Return A/c ₹900 to cancel the wrong credit, and Credit Ganesh's A/c ₹1,800 (reversing wrong debit of ₹900 and recording true credit of ₹900).

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Credit purchases from Neha of ₹10,000 were recorded in the Purchase Book as ₹11,000. What is the rectifying entry?
Option A: Debit Purchases A/c ₹1,000; Credit Neha's A/c ₹1,000
Option B: Debit Neha's A/c ₹1,000; Credit Purchases A/c ₹1,000
Option C: Debit Purchases A/c ₹11,000; Credit Neha's A/c ₹11,000
Option D: Debit Suspense A/c ₹1,000; Credit Purchases A/c ₹1,000
Hint: Both purchases and creditor were recorded with an excess of ₹1,000.
Explanation: Both Purchases and Neha were overstated by ₹1,000 (₹11,000 - ₹10,000). The reversal of this excess requires debiting Neha's A/c ₹1,000 and crediting Purchases A/c ₹1,000.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: The monthly total of ₹100 for discount allowed to customers was credited to Discount Account in the ledger. How is this rectified using Suspense Account?
Option A: Debit Suspense A/c ₹200; Credit Discount Allowed A/c ₹200
Option B: Debit Discount Allowed A/c ₹100; Credit Suspense A/c ₹100
Option C: Debit Suspense A/c ₹100; Credit Discount Allowed A/c ₹100
Option D: Debit Discount Allowed A/c ₹200; Credit Suspense A/c ₹200
Hint: Discount allowed is an expense (normal debit balance) that was mistakenly credited.
Explanation: Discount allowed is an expense requiring a debit of ₹100. Crediting it created an error of ₹200. To rectify: Debit Discount Allowed A/c ₹200 (₹100 to cancel credit + ₹100 true debit) and Credit Suspense A/c ₹200.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: An item of ₹450 relating to Prepaid Rent Account was completely omitted to be brought forward. What is the rectifying entry through Suspense Account?
Option A: Debit Suspense A/c ₹450; Credit Prepaid Rent A/c ₹450
Option B: Debit Prepaid Rent A/c ₹450; Credit Rent A/c ₹450
Option C: Debit Prepaid Rent A/c ₹450; Credit Suspense A/c ₹450
Option D: Debit Rent A/c ₹450; Credit Prepaid Rent A/c ₹450
Hint: Prepaid rent is an asset with a debit balance that was omitted from the ledger opening.
Explanation: Prepaid Rent is an asset carrying a debit balance. Because it was omitted to be brought forward, debiting Prepaid Rent A/c ₹450 and crediting Suspense A/c ₹450 restores the balance and resolves the difference.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Amount payable to Subhash for repairs done to printer ₹180 and a new printer supplied for ₹1,920 were entered in the Purchase Book as ₹2,000. What is the rectifying entry?
Option A: Printer A/c Dr. ₹2,000; To Purchases A/c ₹2,000
Option B: Repairs A/c Dr. ₹180, Printer A/c Dr. ₹1,920; To Subhash A/c ₹2,100
Option C: Repairs A/c Dr. ₹180, Printer A/c Dr. ₹1,920; To Purchases A/c ₹2,000
Option D: Purchases A/c Dr. ₹2,000; To Repairs A/c ₹180, To Printer A/c ₹1,920
Hint: Cancel the entire Purchase Book charge of ₹2,000 and classify into Repairs and Printer Asset.
Explanation: Subhash was credited correctly with ₹2,000 in total (₹180 + ₹1,920), but the debit went entirely to Purchases A/c. Rectification: Debit Repairs A/c ₹180, Debit Printer A/c ₹1,920, and Credit Purchases A/c ₹2,000.
